::: {#exr-miller-int-log-substitution}
#### Substitution leading to a natural logarithm

Adapted from @problifesavercalc, Question 1.1.36.

Evaluate the integral:

$$\int_0^1 \frac{x}{1 + x^2}\,dx$$
:::

::: {#sol-miller-int-log-substitution}
Let $u = 1 + x^2$. Then $du = 2x\,dx$, so $x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}du$.

Transform the limits of integration:

- When $x = 0$: $u = 1 + 0^2 = 1$.
- When $x = 1$: $u = 1 + 1^2 = 2$.

Applying the substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1 \frac{x}{1 + x^2}\,dx
&= \frac{1}{2}\int_1^2 \frac{du}{u} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\sb{\log u}_1^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{2}(\log 2 - \log 1) \\
&= \frac{\log 2}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

*Remark:* When using $u$-substitution with definite integrals, the transformation $x \mapsto u(x)$ must be one-to-one on the domain of integration.
:::
